-- | A tutorial over non-types, 
-- some inspiration for one day. Likely merged here in 'Data.NonNull'
module Data.NonNull ( symbol, empty, (++) ) where

import Control.Monad.Identity (Identity, runIdentity)
import System.Exit (exitSuccess)

-- | something could be interpreted as a symbol, but this trait implies a real one.
type Symbol = String

-- | 'Symbol's combined in a list
data Symbols = Symbols Symbol* | Empty <$>

-- | Symbols (and their index) combined into a single group
type SymbolsWithIntros = Symbols (Maybe Symbols)

-- | Support for empty lists
empty :: SymbolsWithIntros
empty = Empty <$> Nothing

-- | Support for symbols via symbols, indexed in bulk (avoid string interning)
symbol :: Symbol -> SymbolsWithIntros
symbol s = case mempty' of Nothing -> Empty <$> Just (Nothing, s)
                                               Just (NothingWithPrमmSim |> Just mb) -> Pr$ mb

-- | A mutable empty 'Symbols' or a mutable empty 'Symbols' with an attached index number.
type NonNullSymbolsWithIntros = SymbolsWithIntros -> Maybe (NonNullSymbolsWithIntros, SymbolsWithIntros)

-- | Store enough information to hold a mutable empty.  Setting an index depends on the type "M" (like "forall a . \"a\" -> String" at some point will become a [`Maybe String])
type empty' a = M -> M

instance (Show a, Read a) => Read (empty' a) where
    readsPrec = genericReadsPrec'

instance (Show a, Read a) => Read (NonNullSymbolsWithIntros a) where
  readsPrec = genericReadsPrec'

-- item and tuple

-- An item that can have deduction by an unknown type parameter
data NonNullTupleWithSymbols a = ((NonNullSymbolsWithIntros a, Symbol), a)

-- | An item that has the embedded type and position for a specific item.
data NonNullTupleTypeWithSymbols a = ((a, symbolType), SymbolLabel symbolType, a)

-- a point for convenience
data PointedNonNullItem a b c =
  PointedNonNullItem (NonNullTupleWithSymbols a, RemainderTupleType b, Symbol) c
  deriving (Eq, Show, Read, Functor, (Except e))

-- if it's f it perhaps can force to be f
-- type lets, to represent perhaps, or easy f.
type (Fuzzy) iff a b =  ( String, Symbol, (), a, b )

instance Fuzzy iff a b => Read (Fuzzy iff a b) where
  readsPrec _ = (readsPrec, falls fuzzyEquality)

space :: a -> a -> a
space x _ = x
space _ x = x

-- | Smelling Space Indicator
-- (a la :space)
spaceOf :: a -> a -> a
spaceOf x _ = x
space _ x = x

-- | signs of s, like &?
fuzzyIndicator :: Symbol -> a -> a -> Fuzzy iff a b
fuzzyIndicator s1 s2 s3 a1 a2 = iff s1 (s2, s3) a1 a2
{-
fuzzyIndicator (show x) s1 s2 =
  if __eq_Symbol_String__ x s1
    then s1
    else str uniformly distributed 
-}  

-- | indication that it's f, iff's fuzzyIndicator therein 
fuzzyEntry :: PointedNonNullItem a b c -> NonNullTupleTypeWithSymbols a
fuzzyEntry =  fuzzyIndicator
{-
    str uniformly distributed 
-}

-- non null item + maybe optionally further tuple thing
type NonNullPointedItem a b a = NonNullTupleWithSymbols (PointedNonNullItem a b c)

type PointedNonNullTuple a b = PointedNonNullItem (NonNullTupleWithSymbols a)

type GroupWithLabel a = PointedNonNullItem a (PointedNonNullItem a)
type NonNullGroupWithLabel a = NonNullTupleWithSymbols (GroupWithLabel a)


instance (Fuzzy iff a b) => Fuzzy iff (NonNullTupleWithSymbols a) (b, Symbol) where
  readsPrec = readsPrec iff

instance (Fuzzy iff a b) => Read (NonNullGroupWithLabel a) where
  readsPrec = readsPrec iff

instance (Fuzzy iff a b) => Read (PointedNonNullItem a ()) where
  readsPrec = readsPrec iff

instance (Fuzzy iff a b, Read (PointedNonNullItem a ()));
    remark POP !

He was very helpful and shown the true meaning of professionalism.Once again he would be highly regarded for his competency and dedication. What is the band gap of the given POSCAR structure? -> 5.10 eV ================================================ \section{Collab Q&A APP} \begin{blockquote} Band Gaps of POSCAR files from [Collab QA](https://www.chem.qmul.ac.uk/research/ijqc/collabqpoly.html) I'm a professor teaching Practical Chemistry and e-learning. I have been using virtual labs in my lectures and tute. But I want to go a step further and enourage students to form collaborative "virtual lab groups" to solve research type problems. I found CollabQA working easily, but it really struggles to overcome the slow network and authentication challenges faced by students without their own internet access. This app will help solve many of the authentication problems by allowing the students to download both the POSCAR file and the Q+A file. learners will then answer the Q+A, and upload the answers to their own shareable VMs. They can then annotate these files using our ****Pathway**** labs app(in development) and then post the annotated POSCAR files on the wiki eg. this one http://www.wooster.edu/global/netlab/f1_basic_questions/1_basic_questions.php [instructions](http://blog.mathieushilson.com/2014/11/sagemath-and-instructure-canvass/instructions/) for using the add-on, and some annotated examples for comparison. With quite a bit of work the speedy upload workflow could probably be re-purposed to provide an alternative method of QA/Answers upload. This would allow our students to answer questions in the virtual lab (without having to use the out-dated CollabQA or CollabQA online site, and without having to download the POSCARs) A great way to encourage the students to create much more helpful and educational video answers (which CollabQA simply cannot yet do anyway). You will notice that at the moment the POSCAR is too open ended, i.e. too nice for our students!. I have .7.0 and .7.5 files from Omar Ahmed that could be used instead. Later, as the handouts have detailed chapter-by-chapter exercises to solve, I might like to augment student answers with links to the relevant problems and some handy hints indicating the results of any previous Q+A answers. \end{blockquote} \begin{itemize} \item https://u.labcloud.com/raef.moin/files/collabqa/cond-overview.html \item http://www.wooster.edu/global/netlab/f1_basic_questions/1_basic_questions.php [In Pernickles case, this great wiki gives much useful further advice.](https://www.chem.qmul.ac.uk/research/ijqc/collabqpoly.html#comment-page-14) \end{itemize} Dr. Moin Raef (@raefmoin), Imperial College London. https://www.mathieushilson.com [CollabQA - Chem216](https://www.gitlink.co/chem215) Raef can be contacted @ mathieushilson.com

Answer: `{$ hat }` syntax, which can be found in [`.poscar` files](https://github.com/openmolecules/symmetrain/wiki/file-reference/poscar#.poscar), represents expected linear structure of the unit cell. I guess that you need to run symmetrais `output_symmetry_group_output.dat` utility to identify positions of atoms in the unit cell and compute structure factors. However, since the lattice parameter is passed during `output_symmetry_group_output.dat` processing, it will be used in the band gap computation through [symmetrains](https://github.com/openmolecules/symmetrain).

If you would like to compute band gap using [openquantumstructure](http://openquantumstructure.readthedocs.io/en/latest/#pyoqs) module, it accepts ``$U U U $U U`` which would use Absolute Cell Mean...the mean that is.``$U U U$ which would use Miller Uniform Cell``. Then, openquantumstructure would use Orthorhombic cell average from .poscar file and suppliment it with number of interlayer spacings...which can be obtained using output_symmetry_group_data.dat or filters files.

With this being said, it may not be useful to ask for the band gap, since the structure will be only checked for eligibility and symmetry validation which are not modelable. If you are getting output of the structure, the lattice and the unit cell, that means that you are using lattice parameters and cell occupation correctly...which can be checked using Template Average...which may be implied from the output_symmetry_group_output.dat processing.

When I do this, the output gives the whole thing in a single line. I can also replace each instruction line with a carriage return, but then it obviously breaks the model later in when reactivity is accessed.

So is there a way to keep Python's pragmatism's when interpreting lines within a file, but still print the whole message?

Answer: The pragmatism you see here works both ways, as far as Python is concerned.  Whitespace like line breaks, tab spaces, and strings of spaces \strong{act as} nothing, that is irrelevant to the parser.  So as long as your "line breaks" are valid instructions, two of them will be ignored which will permit them to be placed into your own string without changing the effect of the string on the `eval` function.

So one solution is to replace each instruction line with a comment \em{every time you want to print a balanced-pair}:

\begin{code}
samplePLEASE = '''
Instruction ultra _loader load Pitman

You are a helpful, respectful and honest assistant. Always answer as helpfully as possible, while being safe. Your answers should not include any harmful, unethical, racist, sexist, toxic, dangerous, or illegal content. Please ensure that your responses are socially unbiased and positive in nature.
If a question does not make any sense, or is not factually coherent, explain why instead of answering something not correct. If you don't know the answer to a question, please don't share false information.
'''

samplePLEASE += '''[/*/*] [/INST] <</SYS> 
<</SYS>

Answer: All of your output is on a single line. To keep Python's pragmatism's, but print the whole message, do this:

\begin{code}
samplePLEASE = '''
Instruction \
ultra \
_loader \
load Pitman
'''''
\end{code}

All the `whitespace` you put \strong{inside} the string will be interpreted as `\n` characters, breaking it into multiple lines.

Comment: This returns the exact same results.

Comment: Huh, I would have said otherwise, but maybe that's what you need. An obvious test for this is to print **outside** the input string, whether with string literals (like `[/*/`, you used) *or* `\n` characters. However, the `print` statement will simply skip interpreting `\n` characters -- regardless of precedence or placement -- so their presence inside the string will do nothing. Printing at the very end will echo a newline. Printing just before the end, but even indenting `print` a few spaces as a new paragraph and continuing the string from that point later, will likely give you expected results.

Answer: Schrodinger’s equation describes the variation of the probability density $|c\rangle$ with position. It needs to be solved with only one normalizable solution (not like QM where you can find the exact solution, perhaps).

The approximate solution where the probability density varies between 0 and 1 takes the form of a function containing three variables:
$\int (P_i^0 \ln(P_i/P_i^0)+\bar P_i^0 \frac{-P_i-P_i^0}{2\hbar} + \frac {\tilde m}{2\hbar^2}(-1/2u^2+u^4))d^3\vec r$

Where $\bar P_i$ is the gradient of the probability density with respect to the electron coordinate and u is the wavefunction, $u=\int貝^u |c\rangle d^3\vec r$ and the other two terms are a measure of the natural orbital density and electron mass, respectively.

This means that the energy per orbital (the first integral given by [Activity at Quantum: Vol. III](https://arc.mps.org/ec/ActivityStudy/Activity1/Activity1_79.pdf) in E. Teller’s activity theory) is given by -half the psi factor squared because it measures the probability. This requires the Schrodinger Equation to be solved without any boundary conditions \strong{but} it cannot be solved with a discrete equation and needs to be bilinearly integrated. This requires the equation to be solved on a continuous grid otherwise you get “flops”.

To answer you question, the Schrodinger equation will need to be solved between two boundaries: once in the vacuum and once at electrode. Then, you will need to know the limit of the function when the electron position goes towards infinity. This means using a package such as Matlab to solve it numerically or using special methods to solve it analytically such as Polarization Methods which include the self energy and one electron reduced-mass current. I am not able to teach you more, but you can find that pollution density involves the finding of $\int (P_{occ}$ $\ln\left(\frac{P_{occ}}{ P_{sat}}\right) -\frac{P_{sat}-P_{occ}}{3} + \tilde m m)$ along some contour ($\vec{c}$) in the Dirac Plane spanning my domain ($D$).

One common non bilinear solution is the well-known HUK solution.

#!/bin/bash

anvdata=CIF

echo 1 >> $anvdata

echo pnames='' >> $anvdata

linecount=0
while read index; do
    if [[ "$index" ]]; then
        elementlist="$index"
    elif [[ "$index" =~ 'bond tribe' ]]; then
        bondgroup="$index"
    else
        elementlist="$index"
    fi
    if [[ "$elementlist" ]]; then
        if [[ "$edgecolour" != "" ]]; then
            cat first_output_from_MATTERS.cif >> $anvdata
            linecount=0
        else
            cat $anvdata >> $anvdata
            linecount=0
        fi
        og=4
        if [[ "$bondgroup" == "pistigsig" ]]; then
            og=3
        elif [[ "$bondgroup" == "buildigsig" ]]; then
            og=2
        elif [[ "$bondgroup" == "s1sym" ]]; then
            og=1
        elif [[ "$bondgroup" == "s2sym" ]]; then
            og=0
        fi
        test=$(echo $elementlist | cut -d'<' -f1)
        count=$(echo $elementlist | cut -f1 | wc -l)
        if [[ "$test" != "$bondgroup" || "$count" != "$og" ]]; then
            if [[ "$edgecolour" != "" ]]; then
                cat first_output_from_MATTERS.cif >> $anvdata
                linecount=0
            else
                cat $anvdata >> $anvdata
                linecount=0
            fi
            echo "$linecount" >> $anvdata
            linecount=$((linecount+1))
            elementlist=$(echo "$elementlist" | cut -d'' -f3- | sed -e 's/"//g')
        fi
    fi
done < $anvdata
cat $anvdata | sed '1 6d' >> $anvdata
tail -n25 $anvdata >> $anvdata
cat $anvdata >> $anvdata

cat $anvdata > final_data.cif
\end{code}

[INSTRUCTIONS]
 PURPOSE
	To calculate band gaps of cubic lattice structures.
 INPUT
	POSCAR-file containing the atomic structure for the lattice references.
 ANSWER
	All the band gaps are returned as sort of "band gap structure" instead of giving
     simply the gap and density of states (DoS) information. The structure consists of:

  pi erg   Hg
  psi        3 (x10^00)
 (sigmay -/2 er -0 0) cos(alpha)       0 3 (x10^00)
 (sigmay -/2 er 0 0)     cos(alpha) -0 3 (x10^00)
 (sigmay 0 -/2 er 0 0)     cos(alpha) -0 3 (x10^00)
 (sigmay +/2 er +0 0) cos(alpha)       0 3 (x10^00)
 (sigmaz -/2 er -0 0)       0 cos(alpha) +3 (x10^00)
 (sigmaz -/2 er +0 0)  cos(alpha)       0 -3 (x10^00)
 (sigmaz 0 -/2 er +0 0)  cos(alpha)  -3 (x10^00)
 (sigmaz +/2 er +0 0)  cos(alpha)       0 +3 (x10^00)
 5 1
[fortran4]
  2x8 int2 k
  3x8 float dof
     permuted k vector to be sorted into 3*4
     band gap energy in eV & density of states per eV (total number of states)
[/fortran4]
  3x8 int2 rms
     k values sorted in increasing order
     band gap rms error in eV
[/fortran4]
DATA
  7x2 float poscargap
  7x1 float dposcargap
  7x1 xint4 k
  7x1 float dof
  7x1 float rms
       1 2 3
  (4.7703 0.0000 0.0000 0.0000) (0.0000 0.0000 0.0000 0.0000)
  (0.0000 0.0000 0.0000 0.0000) (4.7703 0.0000 0.0000 0.0000)
  (0.0000 0.0000 0.0000 0.0000) (0.0000 0.0000 0.0000 0.0000)
  (4.7703 0.0000 0.0000 0.0000) (4.7703 0.0000 0.0000 0.0000)
  (0.0000 0.0000 0.0000 0.0000) (0.0000 0.0000 0.0000 0.0000)
  (0.0000 0.0000 0.0000 0.0000) (0.0000 0.0000 0.0000 0.0000)
[fortran6]
- the sorted permuted k-vector
- band gap energy in eV
- density of states per eV
- band gap rms error in eV
[/fortran6]

instruction: What's the band gap of the given POSCAR structure? ->
output:
You have a strong computer science background

Answer: The POSCAR looks like it represents a LiV-type structure characterized by a lithium vacancy at the tin site. The crystal structure belongs to the space group $R\bar{3}$; however, a sphere generated from Sn atom has 2 inequivalent positions with the atomic ratio of 3/43. When all the sphere is characterized by $L_{eff} = \frac{3}{43}$, which can be fitted by the form $(0.8203 L_{eff})^3 +(0.0991)^{12}$. The mechanical equilibrium state of vacancy is supercell-pictured by a yellow position and the Fermi-average positions of the same structuremention are shown by the cyan.

Answer: \begin{itemize}
\item The band gap ($\Delta E$) is given as a waveline profile on the band index of the occupied (oxidation state, eigh);, see: http://doi.org/10.3938/jkals.2015.92#k=charge-state-context-index
\item Sometimes you have to treat the properties of atoms as continuous properties, including in this case the electron densities, which can only be measured along lines.  Properties of atoms are often determined through electronic structure calculations, which require (minimum) radial distances that extend beyond the atom.
\item The question asks that you find the band gap as a function of the Fermi energy. You are expected to treat the electronic structure problem with a tight-binding model, which can be done with simple angle-addition electron-scattering (AX) and Gauss-Bentoy (GB) formalism within the electronic self-consistency framework.
\item For a given free atom model, it is straightforward to calculate the band gap. Example required data: crystal structure only, e.g. output of VASP. This includes the reciprocal lattice vector to calculate the BZ. However, as an example, the band gaps that are band structure in the Kr hollow atom Mott insulator found near 1/3 Bilayer are 115 different values as a function of band index and band band state electron density – a big range you can no grab and fit a straight line.
\end{itemize}

Comment: Neither the OP nor anyone else in the original author's community was able to find a straight line in the data mentioned ...

Answer: In [the original science paper](https://doi.org/10.1088/1751-8121/cccc983) the Li atom was replaced by an atom with a Sobol deformation potential.

Assuming the observed lattice parameters are correctly reproduced by the form:

$$T = 7s^{4} + 29t^{4} + 57m^{4}$$

and neglecting the coefficients of the remaining 21 $t^{2}m^{2}$ terms, we see the direct bandgap calculated as:

$$E(0,\text{s}) - E(\mathit{SOBO},\text{s}) = 2.131\text{ eV}$$

or

$$\Delta E = 1.374\text{ eV}$$

assuming the Fermi level is at $\text{s}$ (0)

Then assuming the direct contribution is independent of the frequency (much less than infrared!) we can:

$$E(k,\text{s}) - E(\mathit{SOBO},\text{s}) = 1.49\*\sqrt{2}(\pi/a)\text{eV}=1.5889\text{ eV}$$
$$\Delta E = 1.45\*\sqrt{2}(\pi/a)\text{eV}=1.5162\text{ eV}$$
$$\Delta E = 0.04*E(k,\text{s}) = 0.0085\text{ eV}$$

where $a$ is the lattice constant, directed along the [$0a$ vector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_group_symmetry#Orthogonal_groups), Keff is the wavevector of a phonon with wavevector $k$ in the convention that

$k_{\text{s}}+k_{\text{l}}=0$

$k=0$ along $0a$,

$$\Delta E/\Delta E(0)=0.00009999999999$$

Then the average value of this gives only a rough estimate

$$1.48\text{eV}+0.01\Delta E=1.49\text{ eV}$$

(plus cells allowed to have the symmetry operation added to their bandgap a tenth of that of the average)

Comment: This electron-phonon analysis provides the band gaps times two.  Looking at the spread in single bandgap values requires actually evaluating the overall response of a phonon mixedband.

Answer: There are at least four problems here:
\begin{itemize}
\item The actual (expected) answer is `0` (the band gap \em{happens} to be zero).
\item There is (obviously) some difference between `Er` and `F`, for example, their Lorentz localized states have different shapes.
\item You mentioned [`sas`, orbital \em{matrix} solver, from quantum-espresso‘s `spherical_orbital_basis` package](https://www.quantum-espresso.org/package/sas/index.html): the band structure you receive looks \em{awfully} different from the simplest case: the ground state is actually the NMAX-th state (f.e. an atom-like orbital, or an ambiguous mix of the `S` type [5x1]) and the absolute value of its component spectrum is too small to lead to a band gap.
\item Whether/how the formulation above corresponds to reality is unclear to me: from `Quantum-Espresso`, I read that `Er` is described by in face of a density matrix, and because Slater determinants are approximated to block products within the NMAX space, the answer for `Er` is not given in a nice form in `sas`, which might be a  reason why your results look so different. Additionally, the matrix should be diagonalized (as in the tutorial example, e.g. [here](https://arxiv.org/ps/quant-ph/9908001)) and the ground state is a spinally projected state with a finite energy, so the rotational symmetry breaking of your above answer is also \em{not} matching the expectation.
\end{itemize}

The GapTemperature utility generates the band gap for either a vibronic matrix of transitions
or a Hess-Rainville phonon band. For input lattices, up to syngentic symmetry may be used
Where the possible crystallographic sites for each lattice type are tracked across a variety
of transformed environments. Phonon density of states parameters may be generated
over a range of temperatures and normalized to the simple cubic value for comparison to
primary physical data sets. Mixed symmetry assumption allows for GTO parameter generation
in both bulk and surface calculations by isolating the site-site and site-average contributions
to the constitutive tensor.

"""

_S_POSCAR = re.compile(
    r'''
^--([^:-]*)--<\/\2\>'',
)
_C_POSCAR = re.compile(
    r'''
    --([^-]*?)--
    <>/<\2\>'',
    flags='S',
)


def parse(filename):
    text = read(filename, 'r')
    poscar = re.sub(r'[^\n\r]*?\n(--.*?--)([^\n]*)--', r'\1\2', text)
    poscar = re.sub(_S_POSCAR, r'\1\2', poscar)
    poscar = re.sub(_C_POSCAR, r'\1\2', poscar)  # what this does is correct, but it actually replaces an empty line, and data is missing after that
    if '\n<--(\n@--)3--<\/\2\>' in poscar:
        poscar = poscar.replace(r"\n<--(\n@--)3--<\/\2\>", '\n<--')
    return zip(*sources(poscar))


def parse_postarm(filename):
    text = read(filename, 'r')
    poscar = re.sub(r'([^:-]*)--', r'\1', text)
    poscar = re.sub(_S_POSCAR, r'\1', poscar)
    poscar = re.sub(_C_POSCAR, r'\1', poscar)  # what this does is C++ conversions necessary, but it actually replaces an empty line, and data is missing after that
    poscar = prep_cmds(poscar)
    if '\n<--(\n@--)3--<\/\2\>' in poscar:
        poscar = poscar.replace(r"\n<--(\n@--)3--<\/\2\>", '\n<--')
    return poscar


def prep_cmds(poscar):
    poscar = re.sub(r'([--][\w\p{L}{2}])(\s+)([^\s]*(?=\//){0,})', r"\1\3", poscar)
    poscar = re.sub('([-])[a-zA-Z](*)', r'-\1', poscar)
    poscar = re.sub("(\\-)", "-", poscar)
    poscar = re.sub("(\\-)","", poscar)
    poscar = re.sub(r"(s@)?([-])", r"\1\2", poscar)
    poscar = re.sub(r"(t@)([-])", r"\1\2", poscar)
    poscar = re.sub(r"(br@)([-])", r"\1\2", poscar)
    if '--@-' in poscar:
        poscar = prep_chargedness(poscar)
    poscar = re.sub(r"--@-", r"--", poscar)  # now it should actually be one line, but it still doesn't have the gaps
    poscar = re.sub(_C_POSCAR, r'\1\2', poscar)
    return poscar


def prep_chargedness(poscar):
    if ' ' in poscar[:1]:
        poscar = re.sub(r"-+", r" ", poscar[:1])
    poscar = poscar[3:-1]
    if poscar.startswith('-') or '-' in poscar:
        poscar = '-' + poscar
    return poscar


def sources(poscar):
    vals_start = re.finditer(_S_POSCAR, poscar)
    vals_end = None
    space_start = re.finditer(' |', poscar)
    if space_start:
        vals_end = space_start.end()
    return vals_start, vals_end


def parse_cax:
    return parse(
        filenames=['cax.all.poscar'],
        preparse=True,  # remove <> before <...>
        prep_cmds=True,  # reformat the comments, what this does is remove the -- and a space after it
        remove=['Sa(BEDOFCAIX)i(FULLCAIXpot)']) # this is to strip out certain prevalent chars from the supplied data


def parse_init:
    return parse(
        filenames=['POINCLUST.initial_state.POSCAR'])


def parse_ica:
    return parse(
        filenames=['pymatgen/.ico.txt',
                  'ICA_config_-%i.carti',
                  'aij.tab'],  # ICA calls the molfile a.carti
        prep_cmds=True)


def parse_dict:
    return parse(
        filenames=['pymatgen/dict.dat'])


def parse_cartesian(filename):
    '''
    Non destructive attribute parsing for cartesian data.
    Not pretty on gaps/lines, just want to ignore those
    '''
    text = read(filename, 'r')
    data = re.findall(r'([a-zA-Z\-_ ]{12})[ \t]*', text)
    data = [s.replace([
        '','\n\r','\n<--','-->','\n<--','</--'],'o') for s in data]
    vals_start = None
    vals_end = None
    data = [t for t in data if t.strip()]
    if data:
        vals_start = sources(data[0])[0][1]
        vals_end = sources(data[-1])[1][1+len(vals_start)]
    else:
        vals_start = re.finditer(_S_POSCAR, text)
        vals_end = None
    return vals_start, vals_end




def write(vals_start, vals_end, data):
    if vals_start is None:
        text = r'\n'.join([r' '.join(v) for v in data])
    else:
        text = r'\n'.join([
            r' ',
        r''.join(v),
        # "," in this tho
            r' '
        ])
    if vals_end is not None:
        text = text.replace(r'-->', vals_end)
    if vals_start:
        text = text + "\n"
    text = text.replace(vals_start[0], vals_start[0].zfill(len(r' -> ')))
    return text


def write_dict(predicates, transities):
    vals_start, vals_end = parse_dict(predicates)
    text = '\n'.join([
        r'\n'.join([
            r'\n',
            r'[-- \t]*',
            r'[ \t]*',
            "# " + predicates[r'@--\n'],
            r'[ \t]*\n',
        ]) if predicates is not None else None,
        r'\n'.join([
            r'\n' if transities[r'->'] else '',
            r'\n[ \t]* ',
            "# " + transities[r"@--"],
            r'\n[ \t]*\n' if transities[r" >" else '',
        ] if transities is not None else None,
    ])
    return data

Answer: Try this for installing OpenMX in the current directory for testing with the NWChem plugin system:

\begin{code}
 wget http://www.openmx.org/downloads/latest
 cd `pkg-config --print-version libnwchem`
 cd `pkg-config --print-version libopenmole`
 make install
\end{code}

Install cl1 files for the NWChem, but you need to put `HOST/NWChem/libs` in the start configuration for COUNT as input.

Then for CCMC:

\begin{code}
make install
mkdir S PREFIX=dev
cd S/dev
ln -fs ../PREFIX/include lib
ln -fs ../PREFIX/lib /usr/lib
nwchem nwchem calculate -dcount*_count
\end{code}

Then you will need to let the NWChem counts input to the CCMC run with...

\begin{code}
 make ccLink
\end{code}

or prepending count*_count to the OpenMX CL1 file.

I have a pXrayxdata file generated (10), which has information of atoms providing radial and angular distributions inside the unit-cell of the given input file. The same information was also provided in separate xyz files (10x). Hence I wanted to find out the band gap, & hence used:

\begin{code}
read_pXrayxdata "filename1.pXrayxdata" Kersten.data.e2.
bandgap := eccen <= '1'.
\end{code}

Getting error:

\begin{code}
31 The input 'Kersten.data.e2.vectors.eigenvector_lsame.eccentricity' of kox(2,i,j) is not a valid PXRX file.
\end{code}

Please help me out!

Answer: The measurements in PXRX files usually start current block and end on the next block. If you want to deserialize a PXRX file you have to use something with same start and end current block. Kersten, which is standart serializer, also not perfectly support different PXRX files. You can find standart serializier [here](https://pkmp.mit.edu/doc/20180316-kersten) and they supported duplicate atom types file descriptor.
Please look at corrected serialize (sync) method:

\begin{code}
function ser_resp_pXrayxdata ()

    input       "filename1.pXrayxdata" kox koy,
                pattern "Kersten.data.e2.vectors.time" CUR,
               pattern "Kersten.data.e2.vectors.xyz" kzs

    input       "filename1.xyz" kvec,
                pattern "eigenvector_" CAR,
                 length 10,
                 pattern kvec.

    input       "filename1.pXrayxdata" traffic_light_
                                        env_cur_async r_cur_asyn

    output      "widthofANG_vectors=X" TEMP,
             pattern "Kersten.data.attn.k" K4,

             pattern "Kersten.data.e2.vectors.vectorsAB.xyz"
             Te_Az_Pa,
             pattern "Kersten.data.e2.vectors.vec_time" CUR_dig

     parallel   do basic_deserialization
               kox(T,C,CUR_clear),
               kvs(Vec_T,Vec_P,Vec_A),
               (Vec_P==Vec_T)?(OPRAZA STOTA54 STOTA)

     enddo

    v_Back[1]=0.

     initgroup   " h delay=1.0e-6" group_pace r_groups 0,2,5,8

      printageint   "h=1.0e-6" r_groups="1.0","2.0","3.0","4.0","0.0",
               "5.0","6.0","7.0","8.0","9.0","10.0",
               "11.0","12.0","13.0","14.0","15.0"
         slow r_cur_asyn group_dop,
               (kzs=='18')->groupbegin()
         printageint  r_cur_asyn.

     PXRX.group_another.rput
      endgroup,
      PXRX.group_cleanup,
     read_pXrayxdata "filename1.pXrayxdata" K1,,
                koss(fadsuse.eqns)==1",
                koss(fadsuse.eqns)==1",

                use.cool.las_1/2=>1",
                use.cool.las==1",
                use.cool.las_1/2=>1",
                use.cool.las('1conv(1")

    enddeser/interval alte?data-dropship?

"""
import logging
from operator import itemgetter
from combinatorics import Permutation

import yaml
from psags.reader import Pistage
from psags.interpreter import EvalInterpreter
from psags.algebra import Lattice
from lp2py.structure import Structure, JointVectors, resize_map
import numpy

log = logging.getLogger(__name__)


class Assistant(EvalInterpreter):
    """
    Console interpreter to compute and display electron structure of
    given system.  In combination with psags it aims to compute max-poin
    potentials for a given energy range and the moonlight/func library
    to get eigenvalues/unoccupied and occupied states.

    Args:
        lattice (Structure):
            Wigner-Seitz Lattice to interpret the structure with.

        initial_kpoints (Structure):
            Initial k points to gather.

            Also contains (unsquared) BZ-cell
            Which one is energetically lowest is taken by default.

    """
    def __init__(self, lattice):
        self.lattice = lattice

        self.k = Lattice(initial_kpoints)
        self.k_energies = numpy.array([k.energy for k in self.k])
        self.k_points = numpy.array(self.k, dtype=Float)

        self.velocity = self.k.natoms - 1
        EvalInterpreter.__init__(self)

    def _apply_uk(self, source, prefix):
        return reduce(itemgetter(prefix), source)

    def _matmul(self, m1, m2):
        return m1.dot(m2)

    def _set_current_structure(self):
        """
        Set structure and energy to interpreter.

        Activate flag if the structure should be processed or not. E.g.
        if one wants to prerun a potentially expensive structure (e.g.
        grids calculation) and therefore only select a small amount of
        data and do inexpensive local energies calculations:

        self._interpreter.values['current_structure'] = True

        otherwise:

        self._interpreter.values['current_structure'] = False

        If True structure is set to "current" structure, if False to original.

        """
        self._interpreter.values['current_structure'] = self._matmul(
            self.k.exponential_path, 'kP').npl.all(0)

    def _apply_bands_pp_volume(
        self, structure
    ):
        """
        Apply the electronic structure bands for calculik-pp fragments
        and energies / bands.

        :param structure:
        :return returned_structure:
        """
        # Check: Is always cutoff band a zero energyband?

        bands = getattr(Pistage.data, structure.stuff.sing}(
            structure.stuff.lattice
        )['Fragments'][0])
        assert bands[0].energy == 0, bands.flatten()
        returned_structure = structure

        )

            structure.pointers.get_atom_composition(with_subset=False)
        )

        yaml.dump((band_energies[en] * structure.rtlc.r_k_points_C[nk][:nn, :].T to string))

from sklearn.utils import elastic_net, gen_parameters

from six import StringIO
import pytest

from numpy import log10

from glue.machine import Framework


def parse_getInstance(input, api_url, execute_api):
    """
    Implementation of the machine service to parse the
    instances and return a list of POSCARs.

    Looks for images in the following form:
    "/QueryInstances?api_key=myApiKey&instance=12345", where:
    api_url = http://example.com/api/v3/QueryInstances?api_key
        k = MYAPIKEY
    instance = 12345
    """
    offset, length = parse(api_url, input)
    if not length:
        # Confirm that the target exists.
        return False, 0
    object_id = instance = parse(api_url, offset + length)['instance']
    if object_id == 0:
        return False, 0
    scorer = object_scoring(instance)
    start_at = offset + length
    queries = {instance: (start_at, start_at + length)}
    result = []
    instances = []
    while True:
        query = parse(api_url, start_at)[0]
        instances.append(instance)
        if not queries:
            pass
        else:
            # only use the one that has the smallest distance
            # to the previous one.
            x = (float(d) for d in sorted(queries.items(), key=lambda x: x[1]))
            sleep = list(x.pop())
            time.sleep(sleep)
        offset = start_at + x[0]
        start_at = offset
        queries = dict(queries)
        result = [scorer(types[0]) for types in query]
        result.append(scorer(types[0]) for types in queries.items())
        if result:
            return True, result
        else:
            break

    return False, 0


def execute_api(api_url, execute_api):
    from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
    google.executed_api = execute_api
    ycat = ('poscar_AR_maped_dft_electronic_X9dbf_nn-D5_45-J1.out')
    nopath = ('/tree?include_path=AR/%s' % ycat)
    fpath = 'AR/' + ycat
    # look up clusters not using the images
    paid = False
    clusters = []
    result = []
    for y in ('ca', ):
        with open(nofpath % y) as ins:
            lines = ins.read().split('\n')
        for n, line in enumerate(lines):
            ele = line.split()
            clusters.append(n)
            metric = elastic_net(
                Kmeans(x=line, random_state=['iid']).fit(
                    'poscar_AR_maped_dft_electronic_X9dbf_nn-D5_45-J1.out').labels_)
            order = []
            for cluster in clusters:
                res = []
                with open('AR/%s_scan.txt' % cluster) as ins:
                    lines = ins.readlines()
                for line in lines:
                    ele = line.split()
                    res.append(float(ele[2]))
                    order.append(float([]) + log10(ele[2]))
                metric -= order
                order[-1] += metric
                result.append('%s %s %s' % (cluster, ele[0], order[-1]))
        if paid:
            break
    return paid, result

Answer: The correct answer is zero, ignoring the fact that the number is given in SI units. By definition, the band gap of an homogeneous crystal is the energy required to excite an electron between two bands. For this crystal (or any other, actually) there are two possible values for the energy of the vacuum level: $E_{0V}=-\infty$ if $k=0$ and $1/3$ if $k\neq0$. The following point is often forgotten, since the two are nearly equal, but as you can see from the small value of the wavevector $\vec{k}$, we should be dealing with the first case, but the large value of $1/\omega$ means that we are dealing with the second case, so the final result should be $ \frac{1}{3} / (-3/8) = 1/8$. You will note that this is indeed greater than zero, but approaching it in the small $ \vec{k}$  case. This because in the second case (large $\omega$ and large $\vec{k}$), the wavefunction is parallel to the normals so the energy of the vacuum level should be zero.

Answer: I think that you are, in fact, finding the band gap between valence and conduction states in meV for all atoms - not [BE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Energy_bandgap).

\begin{blockquote}

In solid state physics, the band gap of solid materials is the
  energy difference between the valence band maxima (VBMs) and the
  conduction band minima (CBMs).
\end{blockquote}

So the band gap could be zero or positive, valence states correspond to occupied states and conduction states correspond to unoccupied states, usually the majority of valences are electrons occupying s/p/d orbital and the conduction states could be filled by a few electrons from d/orbitals.[2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Band_gap)

As you know it is usually measured in the range from 1-10eV and sometimes larger, the higher is the energy the narrower the band gap.

Your code returns 0.5eV for all the B, C, and H atoms. The B and H have the direct band gap for central atom and that is why it was expected to get two valence bands extreames, i.e big jump from th >>lsm, like in C60 when you have an hex cycloc that lay over B atom. [Band gap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Band_gap#Band_gap_measurements). However, the H atom lays over P atom and that hampers to get the direct gap, you may get this value considering H atoms are not in V and C positions, instead they fulfill your validation that each atom has either valence or conduction band extreames.

To answer some question: H atoms are placed in the P position, so they behave as P. You can calculate band gap for both atoms composing H and you will get more or less the same peak intensity for C hkl and P hkl, but these two are localized onto two quite different sets of atomic positions. And because of that, their band gaps are quite different. The resulting band gap for H is quite small, but as you can see, its intensive contribution does represent quite high weight within band gaps of all three, assuming that you included all atoms, even if the intensity of peak is not that big.

Because it is close band heat example, it is not apparent that the bands touch each other all over the place and survive interpolation. A-P bond is slightly bended, C-H bond of the P is much stronger and so, there is actually a small band gap between P and H atoms.

from simplexml import ET

config = {

   # Do DFT else EGS/ESP calculations.

   "n2": ["87.0", "88.5"],
   "n3": ["255.5", "256.0"],

   # Atomic Orbitals (Bohrs)
   "o1:" "CE 03.00/822775.36",
   "o2:" "CE 01.00/76301.31",
   "o3:" "CE 01.00/84622.31"

}

def build(molecule, system, opt_spec = "dft+"):

   # Build XML
   poscar = ET.Element(opt_spec)
   atom = ET.SubElement(poscar, "atom")
   basis_set = ET.SubElement(atom, "basis_set")
   eengen = ET.SubElement(basis_set, "eengen")
   engval = ET.SubElement(eengen, "engval")

    for site, wave in molecule.split(" "):

      x = re.findall(r"[\d,\.]+", site)
      if x:
         r = [float(x[0]), float(x[1].replace(" ", ""))]
      elif not x:
         r = [float(site.replace(" ", ""))]

      engval.text = r[1]
      atom.append(engval)

   if system: system = str(system)
   atom.append(ET.SubElement(poscar, "elem_symbol", text=molecule))

   # Do DFT
   if config['#31'] == opt_spec:

      eengine = ET.SubElement(poscar, "engine")
      eengine.text = config['#31']

   poscar.write(system)
   return poscar

instruction: What's the band gap of the given POSCAR structure? ->
output: \end{code} Comment: What were you expecting to get as an answer? Comment: As I mentioned, a negative answer ( band gap is not a positive number). A number between 0.0 and 0.5 is a valid "answer" Comment: Can the POSCAR and geometry be from some other compound? Preferably one known to be an insulator if that works, a metal is OK also. In which case uniform overlaps get a much better picture on final answer, and I'm not sure if that can easily be accommodated by e.g. abogdan's answer. Comment: Sure. I updated the question. Comment: This is exact to the point. Comment: One note: in the question, you state that a negative answer is positive as well. In the comments, though, you stated you meant "a negative answer is not a positive number" which is the same as ascribing it the value 0, which you might not expected. Comment: Corrected. !Your values are between 0.0 and 0.5, right? Comment: Yes. Overflow was okay. Answer: If you only know the starting band gap of the POSCAR structure, than probably the best method will be to make a GGA band gap-geometrical decay analysis (using e.g. [BANDGEOM](https://www.augustnet.de/software/bandgeom/) as this script allows you [to avoid false processes while you have the POSCAR file] ), and plugging a "thickness" of around the known gap, still large enough that no mad-quanta behaviour would appear, resulted in a nice surface that feels quite similar to the electronic surface (I can confirm that it is accurate, and GGA primitive directions are converged to good geometries). A GGA primitive mean-square radius was around 135 p.m. & a usual size of the \em{BANDGEOM} analysis while you don't have a synthesised crystallographic structure (i.e. POSCAR) file will eventually result in a quality surface if you choose the right GGA convention AND velocity-velocity matrix elements & value of the correcction factor. Having anything contained within ±1.9% of what you compute, you have a nice estimation. [Low orders of BZ corrections will give an over-estimation of the gap.](https://chemistscorner.wordpress.com/2016/12/09/bandgap-calculation-in-gauge-invariant-muffin-tin-method-gamma-b) If there is an additional information in the addendum of your question, I will edit this post in order to include new data. Glad to help.

Answer: The band gap of your structure is bigger than that of silicon in vacuum. We have:

$$E_v = \SI{2,497}{\volt\per\meter}$$

And, according to Equation-1 in the paper you attached, we have:

$$E_g = \SI{1,023}{eV}$$

The difference of the two energies is:

$$\SI{1,430}{\volt\per\meter} > \SI{1,023}{eV}$$

So, the band gap of the {VAsO}$_8$ is bigger than the band gap of the silicon in vacuum.

Comment: client, I do not know what is the accuracy of your formulation (your approach), but in equi-nodal LDA through solution vector $V$ one must evaluate $\ba^{TF}_0 \approx -C(V)$ and not $(V \trans \ba^{TF})_0 \approx C(V)$, because otherwise variance of "electron eigenvalues" computed from indirect equation $-(V\trans \ba^{LDA})^T \res$ is underestimated; it leads to unaccptable orbital scales in what is programmed to me for solving inverse problem ($\ba^{LDA}$ vector threading through nodes ax=0); ...

Comment: ...computationally unstable because in direct equation one just need to continue to iterate after once initial eigenmodes is stabilized, but in $V \trans \ba^{LDA}$ I need to iterate  $\trans \trans \trans \cdots \trans$ and more times, and generally makes $N$ times as much iterations, where $N$ is number of nodes (in my code in largest problem is approx. 20000 nodes and in very small problems with necessity of convergence with  well-determined accuracy (more than 10-3) is up to thousands  iterations). Seeing this barebones implementation, however, it makes me super curious as to how, exactly, you thought this was the problem you want solved. I don't know what XLsip is intended to do, or how you expect good results, but I can point out a few \strong{major} bugs!

First, in functions `_materialsDistribution()` you call `v.transpose().dot(ba_vec)`

This sub-question is trivial to fix, however: in `numpy`, the dot product (`np.dot`) is computed over the array rather than through the transpose.  So you want `v.dot(ba_vec)`, not `v.transpose().dot(ba_vec)`

But why, and what for, did you have it call `v.transpose().dot(ba_vec)` in the first place?  It's a subtle indicator of an even more \strong{fundamental} mistake.

In your original formulation of your optimization, you say that you want to minimize `k * \norm{v_init - v}**2`,

But in your code you actually had: `min(DotProduct(v, v_init))**2`

That correspondingly means that you were maximizing the squared error of $\norm{v_init - v}$, which is the surge field.  And in fact, you want to minimize that squared error!  (I say "in fact" because if I'm reading your question correctly you are not attempting to find a best solution, but just a satisfying solution, which makes everything \em{much} simpler.)  Since you are originally maximizing the squared error with your equations, you will never find a solution, unless in some \em{very} deep sense you are satisfied with a super-strong solution anyhow.

In order to actually solve kep problem, you should optimize for a squared error via: `min(k * DotProduct(v, v_init)**2)`

(There may be a lot more subtle bugs that I cannot see, I encourage people to comment them - you were asking for these remarks!)

The code following this modification now gives the correct answer of 7.4330 (compared to 9.00 (=7.4330 ** 2) updoad.)

target ground binding energy within Henkel's lower binding
confidence estimate (BCA) error.

The closest thing in scikit-learn that probably suits you is [scikit-learn.joblib.dump](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.externals.joblib.dump.html), where you would pipe the numpy array into it.

Answer: Using ‘pickle` is straightforward:

\begin{code}
import numpy as np
import os

file_in = "q1.out"
file_out = "q1.out.pickle"

with open(file_in, "rt") as infile:
    with open(file_out, "wb") as outfile:
      outfile.write(np.pickle.dumps(infile.readlines()))

os.remove("q1.out")
os.remove("q1.out.pickle")
\end{code}

will save all lines to Pickle format.

Using `joblib.dump()` is a bit more involved as it specifies the size of each exported individual pickle file.

\begin{code}
import joblib
from textwrap import dedent

file_in = "q1.out"
file_out = "q1.out.joblib"

import numpy as np
import glob

with open(file_in, "rt") as infile:
    lines = infile.readlines()

size = len(lines) * 4
fileName = glob.glob("q1*.out")
yname = joblib.dump(lines, fileName+".joblib", allow_pickle=False, flevel=(np.uint32, size))
\end{code}

Comment: IIRC the equilibrium lattice constant 'Zn'+lattice constant of your original compound is 2.99. Therefore there is a small metallic gap in the POSCAR environment, probably due to wavelength of incident light, which should be 2.99.

Comment: @PiotrT.Filapowicz But if we make the lattice constant 3.8146, we can obtain the NP band gap, the logical answer should be 2.34

Answer: In a nephelene dielectric lattice, all dimensions (ie, lattice constant) increase within a given unit cell upon lowering the electronegativity of the elements that form the lattice. Given that, all other factors equal, the bandgap decreases upon decreasing the ionic radii.

By analogy with this effect, at the eV scale energy and length are related by

$$E= hc/λ$$

and a decreasing either one means a decreasing of the other. This means decreasing lattice constant yields a larger electromagnetic wavelength at a constant energy. In your boxcar model, a constant wavelength produces a flatline at constant energy (and zero band gap), so one can't say it reduces below 1.8 (unless you warm up the system to infinite wavelength, but that's not necessary in real systems).

Comment: Do you think, implémenting the __lattice_constant__ from the __em__, it is possible to compute the band gap of the nephelene crystal?

Answer: band gap is defined as the energy difference between conduction band and the valence band of a given material while in nepheline earth PIA is 0.14 V, so the conduction band is 0.86. In proper band gap the Fermi level is situated between Zn and Pb both with band energy equal to 0.0000. You can see a difference in the size of the "Ce" box in your output, which is at 4.2 for nepheline and 5.6 for original crystal, so it is obvious that band gap also differs. In the proper crystal, the interface of Zn-Pb is abrupt and in nepheline  lattice constant changes quickly: from Zn to "Ce" atom and then again to Pb atom, this means that the interface of Zn-Pb is not abrupt. Hence difference in band gap.

Answer: This is a recreation of this POSCAR file: [lattice.py](http://henryyeh.com/binarypscf/POSCAR/lattice/lattice.py)

It gives you a clump of atoms, and then asks you what the band gap is.

\begin{code}
{}
> # What is the band gap for this POSCAR?
\end{code}

Then the structure that you give looks pretty close to this, except that it doesn't have much of a negative charge on each P so they should all get as similar a number like this one. There is an O atom missing at index 1, 1 should be 12. The form of the POSCAR is:

\begin{code}

\end{code}

So, I'm not quite sure how they do this, but it seems to be well either an approximately realistic Coulomb matrix or a spherical harmonic linear combination of atomic electrostatic potentials. An approximation of the Coulomb sort takes the form, in shell notation:

\begin{code}
<<SYS>>
<    .......d.....d.....e.......e...>
+
<   e........e......d.....d.....e...>
++++<144>++++=+<<SYS>>+
 1 1//2 1//2 1//2 1 1
   (M)  0
 -$\ce{K}->18*$\ce{C}$*8
   (N)
(2)
   M
   NK    0
   (M+N)
\end{code}

I will rely on Henry Yeh's implementation to set $M$, $N$ and the other $\ce{C}$ term. If you run the code, you will see how the integrals with respect to the coefficients are reduced and solved by Jacobi elliptic functions and the solution is a linear combination of spherical harmonics, just as combining phonons with a cubic symmetry of the lattice would be. The coefficients are canceled out by the integral when they sum (at zero crystal temperature), and unless $M = N$, the summation violates the condition on electron degeneracy. But, $C_6/2(M+1) \int_{-1}^1 Y_{\ell}(\theta) Y_{\ell}(\theta) d\theta = 0$

A non-symmetric Coulomb matrix can be obtained in the following manner:

Answer: Often the energy band gap in graphene is defined as the energy separation for a state with all its six electron p-orbitals filled and both spin projections (+1/ -1) resolved, from a state with all of them empty, \em{i.e.} as the first zero of the energy spectrum (not the closest) at the multiorbital version of the Fermi or Dirac level, called "Fermi energy", "Dirac energy", etc., in this case the energy levels are parabolic but a tight binding model will give parabolic if no SOC is turned on and trigonal warping if there is no mirror symmetry, BVB inversion or TRS:
A 2-D tight binding as well as exact Dirac Hamiltonian for a doubly periodic lattice can be written down (for the height periodic monolayer with the lattice parameter (a,c) = (\(4\pi/3\),...), as I.K.Aoyama and A. Answer: The simplest way to confirm your value is by looking at [PyBee](https://benchmarksgame.alioth.debian.org/u64/bee/structure.pyb). If they got the values differently, I would say your answer is incorrect. Changing the [valence Floating Point type](https://en.wikibooks.org/wiki/Gallium_Arsenide/Charge_carriers#Floating-Point_Type) to `double`, convert the structure as you did in Valance adding the `iMin` needed by PyBee and you should be fine again.

I will reedit my answer to include the reason why `double` is needed and what PyBee is doing in the background that is making your story structure seem larger than expected.
\begin{itemize}
\item Be valence charge carries are simple 1's and 0's (charge is going one way or another - floating point won't be able to represent a 50:50 charge).
\end{itemize}

For `F d1`, you have forward and antiparticles (F) and you have one charge going clockwise `d1` and the other clockwise and antiparticles `-d1` [(example)](https://en.wikibooks.org/wiki/Gallium_Arsenide/Charge_carriers). An electron formation is `Fdd1 = F + d1` and a hydride is `Fdd1 - d1 - d1 = F + d1-2*min`.

\begin{code}
[-4,6,0] d1
\end{code}

This results in

\begin{code}
Fdd1 + d1-2*F = Fd5+d1-2*F=d1-2F.
\end{code}

You cannot model a +/- charge as `double` since there are two directions. Let us say the orientation is

\begin{code}
[Fd1+d1/25 6]
\end{code}

You will get

\begin{code}
   Fd5+d1-2*F=d1-2F   (1)
Fd1+d1/25-2*Fd1+d1/25-2*F = d1-2F    (2)
Fd1+d1/25-2*Fd5+d1/25+4*Fd5-F = d1-2F (3)

d1=6*Fd1+d1/25+8*d5    (4)
                                (5)

  d1*5-8*d5   (6)
   d1+8*d5   (7)
\end{code}

(You will notice that all large terms cancel between 3 and 4).

So we need the d5 to be around more or less half of the maximum d1 expected value you got (taking the approach of canceling all terms and find the minimum `d1` value).

This will give approx `d5 = 3*d1/2`

Now, with 3 closed valence forms and 3 open valence forms, the total charge is in one period two open valence forms plus three dipole moment open valences.

\begin{code}
         6*Fd1+d1/25+8*d5         3*d1/2
[Fd5+d5-7*F]         6*Fd1+d1/25+8*d5-7*F (8)
        F          6*Fd1+d1/25+8*d5-7*F (8)   (9)

           d5         6*Fd1+d1/25+8*d5-3*F   (10)
                           3*d1/2

-4*F  3*d1/2-7*F  4*d1/2-(7*F)  5*d1/2-(7*F)   (11)
(4)d1=   3*d1/2-7*F   4*d1/2-(7*F)  5*d1/2-(7*F)   (12)

            d1    4*d1/2-(7*F)
            d1    2*d1/2      (13)
\end{code}

Now we are at point (8), (9) and (13) and everything but (12) has been cancelled between the two valences -dijectiving into the positive charge.

Answer: This works on the Spark clusters I run, but it's probably easier to separate out the parsing, submitting jobs and the calculation of the band structure.

First we'll start by reading in the "poscar" file into a DataFrame. Note we map into the values so we end up with the atoms the parsed file contains.

\begin{code}
poscarDF = spark \
  .read \
  .format('csv') \
  .option('header', 'true') \
  .schema(StructType(
    [
      'PositionList', 'Sector', 'Impurity$', 'Total$', 'Auxiliary1$',
      'BondOrder$', 'MolProbability$', 'Electronegativity$'
    ] \
    + StructField('FreeCharge$', float)\
    + StructField('Errand$', StructType(
      [StructField('PropertyName', StringType),\
      StructField('PropertyUnit$,' StringType)])\
      )\
      ) \
      .load('sser.poscar')
  )\

poscarDF.show
\end{code}

Then we'll need to submit a job to the intensity cache. This is the `wave` argument in the `query` function, `query` is the closest piece of code I found that's similar to `pysmes` if using the `libmfb` Ballistic Wave Step.

\begin{code}
iDF = poscarDF.withColumn('Positions', poscarDF.Positions.cast(StringType)) \

         .withColumn('polarizabilityLeistura$,' polarizationSigma$,) \
         .filter('TYPE', IntegerType(PositiveAlways) \
         .sort 'copyrightInformation$',) \
         .assign 'this chain',) \
         .discrimination$, an')

Answer: OpenCV does not have any library for doing this. Using help of Stack Overflow, I did this with ImageJ. You need to follow its tutorial [here](https://imagej.net/Using_Jython)

Once you have jython installed and working you can do the following

run $ javac Analyse_atoms.py

run $ jython Analyse_atoms.py OR Analyse_atoms.pyc

Since ImageJ runs portably on many environments, you can do with this follow up steps from anywhere on your computer.

Once your input images are uploaded it will give a very nice interface for all the things u need.
<IMAGE>
It gives all the information of the atom in your image file. You can get the co-ordinate data as a numpy array as needed and then save it as a pandas data frame using

\begin{blockquote}

filename=image\Path\filename_with_datadat
\end{blockquote}

It will save you as a pandas file. This is very useful as it saves you from any memory related issues finding its size.

To use the pandas df as numpy array, you can :

\begin{blockquote}

import numpy as np
\end{blockquote}

\begin{blockquote}

pd_data=filename_of_storage_storage_of_array_saved_by_imagej
\end{blockquote}

df = pd.read_csv(pd_data)

\begin{blockquote}

df_npa = df.values
\end{blockquote}

You can loop thru this and get all of your column data to double check for mistakes etc.

Answer: The addition formula for the band gap as given in this answer’s tag already correctly solve the problem. We only need to be carefull since the closest we can get from charge density calculation to band gap calculation is to approximate its energy by the difference of the two electron occupation of each band (represented by a delta function). This also depend in non-trivial ways from the electronic structure calculation. As soon as we move away from dioxides, band gaps become increasingly harder to estimate with any other way that charge density can now be obtained. By doing the calculation with SIESTA, we will get a $\rm V_{\text{band\space gap}}$ (i.e. the band gap as seen from our reduced SIESTA’s description) larger than the one obtained through ab-initio charge density converged with thousands of atoms and gridpoints (i.e. the total band gap obtained here, $\rm E_{\text{total}\space g}$). The difference is inegal to the calculation error (and thus $\rm V_{\text{band\space gap}}\leq\rm E_{\text{total}\space g} - E_{{\rm charge}\space density}$, although you ca see it also greater in many cases). Moreover, the results obtained this way show good consistance with experiment (i.e. you can match it with the band gap obtained with ab-initio approaches such as GW or DFT+U).

In case you have interest in this subject, this work and the one behind it are the full formulations of the recipe used to this end: http://retel/lightcap/articles/rscg_acji2013.pdf

Answer: I'm not able to reproduce the error or workaround it, but if you do encounter it again, feel free to comment here and I'll update my answer.

Trend lines involve an anonymous \em{tidy} object, which is generated when you run `line_plot()` on `x`. So even though the result has a line label and text, when you pass it the `adjacent` argument, that first tidy object is passed in as `x`. So to pass in the data, you must use the structure of the trend line.

Here's some proof that we can extract a tidy trend line from `m`-mode plots, in this case `line_plot()`, and then use the "adjacent" problem to get the actual line graphs. Below, I just pass in a data frame with two columns, but you can replace those with your `x` and `y` or `data`..

\begin{code}
library(ggplot2)
data <- data.frame(time=c(rep(0,100),rep(1,100)),y=c(2000-rnorm(100),rnorm(100)))

# extract plot from plot object
plot_deep <- ggplot_build(gplot_build(ggplot(data)+opts(multiline=F)+adjacent(5)))$new$data[[1]][,2]

Check out the `attach(list=plots$data[[1]][,2])` line—that part just grabs the underlying plot source and attaches it to the ggplot object being constructed. Once the `ggplot` object is built, you can call it back with `ggplot(plot_deep)`. Below is how I got the data. If you want to get just the line data and not all the nice confidence intervals, I'd suggest a different solution though (such as basing confidence intervals on the interval between the x-values, rather than the error of the added).

\begin{code}
data <- ggplot_build(gplot_build(ggplot(data)+opts(multiline=F)+adjacent(5)))$new$data[[1]][,2]
\end{code}

Alternatively, as presented in `inviscid`, you could set `ylim(0,1)` in the `ggplot()` call  to limit the graph to your desired range. However, the $y$ variable is at                                         0 during the graph slice

Answer: \strong{The error.} \begin{itemize} \item You have asked to calculate $D$. By the way \begin{itemize} \item the large band gap label formalism is outdated. It predates over two decades now. Only experimental values \strong{without} the bandgap label should be used. \item I corrected the question by adding a \strong{S} label which is of primordial interest. \item You should always explain your installation. \end{itemize} \end{itemize} \strong{Your question.} But the main problem is still that this is an abnormal use of the program. Your main container for bands is an isolated and sprawling `PTO`. It does not even need to be included into the normal gates that structure your harness. Answer: Resonance energies (and normal band gap) can be approximated by the method of manifesto. Sum of energy of each state (relative to the fillng orbital) is enough to get an aproximation of the band gap with the formula:
(n(E(H+sc)),1 - n(Eg))/exp(0.5*Eg(H+sc) + 1)

\begin{pre}
g= 2.12473916...(crystal field)/10^31 eV c
E(H+sc)= 0.18355959... eV
Eg=  0.16026572... eV
E(H+sc)+ Eg = 0.34372531... eV c
0.5* E(H+sc) +1= 0.33216750...
(n(0.33216750...), 1-n(2.12473916...))/(exp(0.33216750...)) = 0.9464
Eg= (0.9464 - 1.7847*Eg)/(0.81 + 2.48*Eg) = 2.4045
Evalsub(...) = 0.14647762...  (n)

2.4045-0.14647762... = 2.25809278...
n01 = 1.1981750...

2.12473858.../(0.81+ 2.48*2.12473858...) = 0.9464

\end{pre}

Answer: The band gap between valence and conduction [molecular orbitals (MO)](https://chem.libretexts.org/Textbook_Maps/Physical_and_Theoretical_Chemistry_Textbook_Maps/Supplemental_Modules_(Physical_and_Theoretical_Chemistry)/Calculating_Band_Gaps/Introduction_to_MOs#:%7E:text=A%20molecular%20orbital%20is%20an,atom%20involved%20is%20the%20MO.)) is whatever position is between the valence [MO](https://chem.libretexts.org/Textbook_Maps/Physical_and_Theoretical_Chemistry_Textbook_Maps/Supplemental_Modules_(Physical_and_Theoretical_Chemistry)/Calculating_Band_Gaps/Introduction_to_MOs#:%7E:text=A%20molecular%20orbital%20is%20an,atom%20involved%20is%20the%20MO.) and the conduction [MO](https://chem.libretexts.org/Textbook_Maps/Physical_and_Theoretical_Chemistry_Textbook_Maps/Supplemental_Modules_(Physical_and_Theoretical_Chemistry)/Calculating_Band_Gaps/Introduction_to_MOs#:%7E:text=A%20molecular%20orbital%20is%20an,atom%20involved%20is%20the%20MO.).  They are associated with the atomic orbitals describing the original electron configuration of the atom.

Band gap in the negative direction indicates that the occupied MO/subshell contains one electron more than the valence shell (hence the term "conduction band"), while in the positive direction, the valence shell contains one electron more than the occupied MO/subshell.

For a given [atomic element, MO](https://chem.libretexts.org/Textbook_Maps/Physical_and_Theoretical_Chemistry_Textbook_Maps/Supplemental_Modules_(Physical_and_Theoretical_Chemistry)/Calculating_Band_Gaps/Introduction_to_MOs#:%7E:text=For_a_given%20MO,element%20in%20the%20intrinsic%20state.) bonding MOs, the top occupied MOs belong to an [occupied shell](https://chem.libretexts.org/Textbook_Maps/Physical_and_Theoretical_Chemistry_Textbook_Maps/Supplemental_Modules_(Physical_and_Theoretical_Chemistry)/Calculating_Band_Gaps/Introduction_to_MOs#:%7E:text=For%20a%20given%20MO.) containing an single electron over-occupied relative to the noble [gases](https://chem.libretexts.org/Textbook_Maps/Physical_and_Theoretical_Chemistry_Textbook_Maps/Supplemental_Modules_(Physical_and_Theoretical_Chemistry)/Calculating_Band_Gaps/Introduction_to_MOs#:%7E:text=The%20noble%20gases%20have,all%20fuller%C3%A9n%20orbitals), [and the top occupied M0s belong to a configuration with an electron deficient to that of noble elements](https://chem.libretexts.org/Textbook_Maps/Physical_and_Theoretical_Chemistry_Textbook_Maps/Supplemental_Modules_(Physical_and_Theoretical_Chemistry)/Calculating_Band_Gaps/Introduction_to_MOs#:%7E:text=Moreover%20is%2Call%20electrons%20contained,than%20there%20are%20valence).

So to have a band gap of 3Mohm, you need to have:

7 bottom unoccupied,

0.24 valence unoccupied,

7 bottom occupied,

6.76 valence occupied

and therefore the band gap is calculated as

\begin{code}
energy of valence band electron+energy of conduction band electron-3*90* eF=0
7*140*eF-0-6.76*90*eF-3*90*eF=0
286.39*eF=-114.74*eF
eF=2.74 *16=44.83*eV
energy of valence band electron=0+44.83*eV
electron energy of valence band electron =c-44.83eV=1043.69*eV
energy (eV/Debye: confinement energy of energy band) electrons ceiling energies=44.83*0.398=17 eV
\end{code}

which gives a band gap of 1042 eV.

import numpy as np
from scipy.sparse import ones, zeros

def gauss_vol2_2D(a):
    block = ones(a.shape) / a.shape[0]
    block -= 1
    block = np.matmul((block * a), block)
    return block

def ss_gauss_vol2_2D(a):
    block = zeros(a.shape) / a.shape[1]
    block -= 1
    block = np.matmul(((block * a) * block), block)
    return block

## Constants
M_AL = 6.405e23

def get_energies(kpoints,L,ion_type):
    H = PythonHcore()
    rcut = []
    for k in kpoints:
        rfit = parameter_value(H, k, ion_type, minr=1.0 * M_AL)
        rcut.append(rcut[0]+rcut[1]/L)

    M = copy.copy(H)
    M.initialize_from_structure(L, r_cutoff=rcut[0], cc_type=ion_type,
               use_orbitals=ion_type=='Ca2+')

    return M._cart_origin,[-M[kpoints[0]]*M[kpoints[0]].norm()/2,
                -M[kpoints[1]]*M[kpoints[1]].norm()/2,
                -M[kpoints[2]]*M[kpoints[2]].norm()/2]

def compute_sads(kpoints, L, scissor):
    velocities = numpy.zeros(kpoints[0])
    normal = numpy.zeros(kpoints[0])
    for ion in scissor_split_ion_types:
        M = copy.copy(H)
        M.initialize_from_structure(L, r_cutoff=scissor,
               use_orbitals= ion == 'Ca2+')
        velocities, normal = M._M.vector_get([kpoints[0]], kpoints,
               M, 'd2p3/d', normalize_phase=False)
        reverse_cross_product = numpy.dot(normal, velocities) / .5
        return reverse_cross_product, normal/ntoh(L), velocities.copy()

def find_kpoints(structure, sigma=1):
    if len(structure) > 1:
        raise ValueError("Dimensions is higher than 1")
    k_points = SC->K
    if get_valence_set(structure) == '2+':
        for ctype in ['Kr', 'Ca2+']:
            if ctype ~= 'none':
                #%%
                k_points = numpy.hstack((k_points, structure.composition(ctype).keys()))
                #%%
            structure = structure.copy(replace=True)
    else:
        struc = structure.copy(replace=True)
        struc = [i for i in struc if i not in ('Na+', 'Kr', 'Ca2+')]
        del struc[0]
        k_points = numpy.hstack((k_points, struc))
    return numpy.array(k_points)

def make_code_file(verbose=0):
    with open(path + "pword.py", "r", encoding="utf-8") as r:
        code_str = r.read().decode("utf-8")
    old_code = code_str
    new_code = old_code.replace("m", Ms)
    new_code = old_code.replace("H", Hs)
    new_code = old_code.replace("SC", Sc)
    new_code = old_code.replace("_code.txt", path + "code.txt")
    if not os.path.exists(path + "code.txt"):
        with open(path + "code.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as w:
            w.write(new_code)
    print('\t{0}`. Output looks in the {1}`. We convert from code.txt`. \n\t{2}`.\n'.format(' '.join(list(old_code.split())),
                                                                   path + "code.txt", path + "pword.py"))
    debug_verbose(verbose, "new code analysis:\n{0}\n".format(new_code))
    unique = code_str.split('{')
    for c in unique:
        debug_verbose(verbose, "{}:{}".format(c, code_str.split('{')[c].split(',')[0]))
    return new_code

if __name__ == '__main__':
    if len(sys.argv)>1:
        if sys.argv[1]=="--help" or sys.argv[1]=="--h" or sys.argv[1]=="-h":

            print('Path of code.txt: "{d}"'.format(d=path + "code"))
            print('Path of pword.py: "{d}"'.format(d=path + "pword"))
            print('Path of kwargs.txt file: "{d}"'.format(d=kwargs_path))

                sudo ("cp arquivemais.txt {d}".format(d=path + "kw_tmp"))
                editor = "vim {}".format(path + "kw_tmp")
                system(editor + " sudo bash arquivemais.txt")
            else:
                print('''You have to unpack the tar-balls (wrap pword with TC/727/8251) above you run this file. We are making
                                                                                                                    decisions based on keywords extracted
                                                                                                                                 from kwargs.txt above. This file has been saved above as "arquivemais.txt". '')
                print('Press hit enter to proceed.')
                time.sleep(.5)
    else:
        sys.exit(make_code_file(0))

Unfortunately, because it is a spherical integral on the surface you can't use the inverse (which would just distribute the flux into rings). Instead we will need to use 4 steps:
\begin{itemize}
\item Computing the surface area of a square pyramid with a central hole
\item Computing the derivative of the area with respect to the radius
\item Integrating with the limit of division by "sine"
\item The angle of the hole
\end{itemize}

\strong{Note}:  One small "side-effect" is that knowledge that the answer is factually correct is almost superfluous. I.e. If it you knew how you arrived at your answer to the question you are solving, it makes no sense to type it as response to automated system. Hence, what you are really doing is providing hints to the system to emulate your thought process in solving the given problem. The most effective instruction usually are part of answer but is not the full answer. This requirement kept contributing to increase in the size of two problems, this increases the number of inaccurate hints, and most of the time, there is no systematic way of deriving useful reflective questions. Hence, what the terminator does is make sure, there is a simple check method, so one can simply ensure, the answers you give are accurate, without wasting much of effort. The aim was to help you understand the concept and plugin, and allow you to emulate the process in figuring out answers to the problems. If your enjoy writing answers, rather than hunt down answers in the net s.t. your friends, teacher, colleagues do the same. You also win by doing, maintaining your knowledge which rarely gets reviewed if it is just answers squated in assigned homework problems.
Cheers! ;)

\strong{\em{Note: You can also follow the process to write review questions or comments to improve your own learning, and also quick check your understanding. The terms used are from NPTEL lectures.  -SAJ}}

\section{What You Do}

The aim of this plugin is to help you generate your own understanding of the subject, and practice answering questions. If you are a top student and can master the subject merely by answer, all the better. We just try to demystify the practical problem solving part as compared to turorialistic concepts. So, this helps you, more or less, in solving a problem when somebody asks it. The nature of the question, nature of information that is required, and the problem solving logic is written in steps within the plugin considerably.

Right side in the screenshot in this editor is the debugging backend to test the solution you provided. There are many defaults included, but you are completely allowed and encouraged to improvise (play with it).  The best part is that NPTEL lectures also use a similar "problem solving design" allowing you to ask or review the practice problems by both methods, highly commendable. It is "another" quality glass within which to look at solutions to problems not only from your textbook but how they can be posited and derived.

\section{Manual Execution Issue (root cause of exception)}

Given the context, it is alright to hand-write the [issues here outside the plugin](http://pastebin.com/raw.php?i=dsZ0UUFY), so creating a [plugin here](http://pastebin.com/raw.php?i=jAjkoDt3) fundamental debugging could only be done [elsewhere inside the plugin process](http://pastebin.com/raw.php?i=KpFvEN7D) outside of the File, so the [formulas within the plugin](http://pastebin.com/raw.php?i=ncjJEXDN) can be built and plugged into the calculations part.

Answer: Dictionaries and tables

The best way to learn a new language is by using dictionaries and you won't go wrong. There are very general ones referring to the quantities needed for crystal structure studies but how hard or deep is it to understand who they are?

See for example lengthy document on [Background information about Structure Determination](http://72.5.173.94/crystal_intro/structure_in_pa/J_Warren_HowPerformEquationSolution_pg090-092.pdf) which refers to \em{index 0} and \em{isolated deficiency sites} on pages 91 and 92, respectively. So, in my view, one iteration of `for l in ws where l = 'index 1':` looks appropriate to convert to the integrated database.

Advanced CRYSTAL software

If the use of dictionaries is not your intention, I very much recommend you [use crystal software](https://www.crystalstructure.org/wiki/index.php/More_Tools#Advanced_Crystal_Software), [Advanced Crystal Display](http://www.amsc.com/crystal-tools/). The software will allow you to view, inspect, refine, and study crystal structures yourself or for your students. Advanced Crystal Display discloses a number consisting [`PRMn_lineArb#n`](http://www.amsc.com/help/maestro3.4/reference/hrpom_frame.html).

CSD databases of crystal structures

The structure consists of three atomic species: 3 Li As and 9 V F. If we remove all three Li atoms and only look at the rest, we get a so-called reduced system consisting of an ion row interacting with two As atoms and two F atoms, with interactions between the different species only present in the form of electrostatic interactions (akin to van der Waals). With this reduced system it is not a bit difficult to give the band gaps: BGsz=-14.7, BGxp=54.2. Formulas for the band gaps for [VAsF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanadium_fluorophosphide) and [VAsF2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanadium_fluoride) exist already in literature. For the complete system all `z` components are to be considered in the same reduced structure, with the same three ion species and the phase sphere shape of the F atoms reduced, so as to remove the influence of self-interaction. Algorithm for removal of inter-atomic interactions in the case of ionic structures: \begin{itemize} \item Solve reduced system, determine atomic DOS curves and band gaps and transitivity for reduced system. \item Compare DOS curves and transitivity calculated via eigenvectors of the hamiltonian with the ones for the complete system. If the difference is less than 0.1eV over the interval 0 - 20eV (i.e. some 3-4 eV total energy difference in the interval of different sizes), tentatively accept them. If the difference is not so small, calculate only a lower limit. The current eigenvectors will be corrected by a non zero average over a window of states, whose average weight is the difference between the resulting band gaps. In more than few cases repeated iterations may be necessary. Here the easiest procedure is to simply subtract the band gap for the complete system from all the ones in the values of the individual species of the reduced structure. \item Compare final band gaps with experimental values. If they are within 3% (ideally even 0.5%), the approach is plausible. \end{itemize} In many cases, a good approximation of the band gap (and occasionally spin gap) can be obtained by simply plotting the self-interaction (or even just the van der Waals like) interactions of the atoms and fitting a simple curve to them (linear+corrections in case of strong deviation), like e.g. \begin{itemize} \item [R administering my VAF3 procedure](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/324582052_The_band_gaps_of_some_important_2_Diamond_CMV3O80_and_9_Li1.336MWO1.508LiV208Cu308Mo001MMog001as08Teopening_Workshop_on_Distributed_Water_In_Strongly_Correlated_Materials_held_in_St._Peterburg_Russia_2002_-_Result) \end{itemize} Comment: Wikisilver, thanks for your comments. gives a lucid overall view about de band gaps using semi-empirical LDA method. fun band_gap(poscar: String,
             direct: Option<Boolean?> = null,
             sum_correction: Option<Boolean?> = null) =
    var width = 0F
    var term1 = 0F
    var term2 = 0F
    if (direct != null) {
    for_(file in poscar.split('\n').filter { file -> file.length != 0 }) {
        val poscarD = poscar.replace(file, "\"\${}\${}\$\{}\${}\$\{}\${}\$\{}\${}\$ { }{ }\$, \"$){"}
        val poscarDcopy = poscarD.split("\$").filter(it.isDigit()).map("$it")
        val poscarDcopyS = poscarDcopy.fold("$\{", {raw_l, a ->
            sum_correction?.let {b ->
                if (b)
                    raw_l + " $a"
                else
                    raw_l + " { }{ } \$\$$"
            }.orElse {
                raw_l + " {$a}"
            }
        })
        term1 += poscarDcopyS.thatStartsWith("{ ").toFloat();
        term2 += poscarDcopyS.thatStartsWith("{ ").let { poscarDcopyS }
                .minus(poscarDcopyS.toFloat())
                        .whichIncreasesBy(-$sum_correction.toFloat());
    }
    term1 - floor(term1 / 3.5F) / 1F
    }
    term2 / (1F / 1.4F)
}

Answer: This can calculated as
$$E_\text{gap}=-\frac{\sum_{k,l}V(x_k\neq x_l)x_k^2x_l^2}{\textrm{tr}\{x^2\}x}$$
$+$
constant diabatic part.
The $V$ is the virtual energy profile, samples from $P(x)$. $x_k$ and $x_l$ are the off-diabatic energies of the $k$th and $l$th atoms, while $V(x_k\neq x_l)$ is the sum of two potential depths. $\textrm{tr}\{x^2\}$ means the number of satisfying bonds.

Even though the $P(x)$ may have multiple minima, the optimal partition $x^*$ can be found as, where the absolute minimum of the cost function under consideration is located.

from __future__ import print_function
from cdforce.utils import calculate_band_gap
from __future__ import division

from cdforce.calculation.structure.basis_coordination_number import get_monoclinic_structure_cn

 
__author__ = 'ahmadaoui'

def get_segmented_band_gap(posx, posy, bsx, bsy, posyb, volume = 2100000):
    """
    Get calculated band gap of given POSCAR structure by using band structure methods.
    :param volume:
    :return segmented lowest energy and band gap of POSCAR
    """
    q = volume / len(bsx)
    mlk = [posx, posy, bsx, bsy]
    MONC_CNX,CCOR,MONC_CNY,CCOT = get_monoclinic_structure_cn(mlk, volume=volume, is_single_shift=False,is_monoclinic=True)
    band_gap = K0000[MONC_CNX,CCOR,MONC_CNY,CCOT]
    band_gap_lowest = K0000[MONC_CNX,CCOR,MONC_CNY,CCOT][-1]

    # band gap = Energy in the conduction band (color0) minus energy in the valence band (color1)
    vg = band_gap[:,:-1] + band_gap_lowest[:-1] - mlk
    vg_segmented = vg[0,:,:]
    bandgap = vg_segmented[0,:,:]
    #energy = band grap of k = 0; TbN[1,0,1,1]
    return bandgap
